rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: When \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) is fused with KOH in air, it gives :
rows.solution:
Fusing manganese dioxide with potassium hydroxide in air gives POTASSIUM MANGANATE, \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\).

Air supplies the oxidising agent, and manganese is raised from \(+4\) in the dioxide to \(+6\) in the manganate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is a dark GREEN solid, and this is the first step in making permanganate from pyrolusite ore.

Potassium permanganate is the trap. It is obtained from this manganate, but only by a SECOND step — electrolytic oxidation of the manganate solution, or its disproportionation in acid. Fusion with alkali alone stops at \(+6\).

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Ligand \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\) is an example of a :
rows.solution:
The \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\) ion is a POLYDENTATE ligand — specifically a hexadentate one.

Count its donor atoms. The ion is \((^-\mathrm{OOC{-}CH_2})_2\mathrm{N{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}N(CH_2{-}COO^-})_2\): two nitrogen atoms, each carrying a lone pair, and four carboxylate arms, each offering an oxygen. That is SIX donor atoms, and all six can bind the same metal ion at once.

Polydentate is the general term for a ligand with more than two donor atoms; monodentate means one and didentate means two, so those three options are simply too few.

Wrapping right around the metal closes five chelate rings, which is why EDTA complexes are so exceptionally stable — and why the ion is used to soften water and to treat lead poisoning.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following ligand forms chelate complex ?
rows.solution:
The OXALATE ion, \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}\), forms a chelate complex.

A chelate is formed when a single ligand binds the metal through TWO OR MORE donor atoms at once, closing a RING that includes the metal. The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE: it attaches through two of its oxygen atoms, and the ring so closed has five members.

The other three cannot. Chloride and ammonia each have only one atom to offer. The nitrite ion has two DIFFERENT donor atoms, nitrogen and oxygen, but it is AMBIDENTATE, not bidentate — it uses one OR the other, never both at once, because the two are too close together to reach the same metal.

Chelation is what gives such complexes their extra stability, an effect large enough to have its own name: the chelate effect.

rows.stem: Which of the following contains \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised carbon bonded to X ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Option (B) is PRINTED AS A DRAWING: a skeletal benzene ring (Kekule, one inner double-bond stroke) with a bond from one vertex to the label "CH2 - X". The other three options are printed as ordinary condensed formulae exactly as transcribed. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The compound with an \(sp^2\) carbon bonded to the halogen is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}X}\), the vinylic halide.

Hybridisation follows from what the carbon is doing. A carbon forming a DOUBLE bond is \(sp^2\); a carbon with four single bonds is \(sp^3\). In the vinylic halide the halogen sits ON a doubly bonded carbon, so that carbon is \(sp^2\).

In the allylic halide the double bond is present but the halogen is on the NEXT carbon along, which is \(sp^3\). The same is true of the benzylic compound — the ring is \(sp^2\) throughout, but the halogen is on the \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) beside it. The ethyl halide has no double bond at all.

The consequence is chemical, not just descriptive: an \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative and holds the halogen more tightly, and the halogen's lone pair is delocalised into the double bond — which is why a vinylic halide is so unreactive towards substitution.

rows.stem: Which of the following is most acidic ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR options are PRINTED AS DRAWINGS and none is named in words. (A) a skeletal benzene ring bonded to the label "CH2 - OH"; (B) the same ring bonded to "OH"; (C) a SATURATED six-membered ring (no inner double bonds, i.e. cyclohexane) bonded to "OH"; (D) a benzene ring with "Cl" at one extreme vertex and "OH" at the opposite one — verified at 2x zoom to be the PARA (1,4) arrangement, the two substituents sitting at opposite ends of the drawn hexagon. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The most acidic is p-CHLOROPHENOL, \(p\)-\(\mathrm{Cl{-}C_6H_4{-}OH}\).

First separate the phenols from the alcohols. Both phenols listed are far stronger acids than either alcohol, because the phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, while an alkoxide's charge is stuck on one oxygen. Benzyl alcohol and cyclohexanol are ordinary alcohols, with \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) around 16.

Then compare the two phenols. Chlorine is electron WITHDRAWING, so it helps disperse the negative charge of the phenoxide ion further, stabilises it, and makes the proton leave more readily. p-Chlorophenol has \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 9.4 against phenol's 10.

Any electron-withdrawing substituent would do the same, and the more strongly withdrawing it is the stronger the acid — which is why picric acid, with three nitro groups, is a genuinely strong acid.

rows.stem: Anisole reacts with HI to give :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — The aromatic half of every option is PRINTED AS A DRAWING — a skeletal benzene ring carrying, respectively, the labels "OH", "I", "CH2 - OH" and "CH2 - I" — with the second product ("+ CH3 - I" / "+ CH3 - OH") set beside it as ordinary text. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Anisole with hydrogen iodide gives PHENOL AND IODOMETHANE.

Cleaving an ether with hydrogen iodide always breaks the bond on the side that can accept the iodide, and here one side is an ARYL group. An aryl-oxygen bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring, so it will not break. The iodide therefore attacks the METHYL carbon instead:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}OCH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The option giving iodobenzene and methanol is the trap — it breaks exactly the bond that cannot break. The two remaining options both insert a \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) that was never in the molecule.

rows.stem: Ethanol on heating with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 413 K gives :
rows.solution:
Ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid at 413 K gives ETHOXYETHANE, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5}\).

TEMPERATURE is what selects the product, and this is the lower of the two standard values. At 413 K the acid protonates one alcohol molecule and a SECOND alcohol molecule then attacks it, displacing water in a bimolecular step; the ether results:
\(2\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

At 443 K the protonated alcohol instead loses water to give a carbocation, which then loses a proton, and the product is ETHENE. That is the trap here — the right reaction at the wrong temperature.

Ethyl hydrogen sulphate is an intermediate on one route to the ether, not the final product at this temperature.

rows.stem: An azeotropic solution of two liquids has boiling point lower than either of them when it :

options.label: B
options.text: shows positive deviation from Raoult's law

options.label: C
options.text: shows negative deviation from Raoult's law

options.label: D
options.text: shows no deviation from Raoult's law

rows.solution:
An azeotrope boiling lower than either component shows a POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

A positive deviation means the vapour pressure of the solution is HIGHER than predicted, because the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are weaker than those between like ones, so the molecules escape more readily.

A higher vapour pressure means a LOWER boiling point — the mixture reaches atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature, so the azeotrope is a MINIMUM BOILING one. Ethanol with water is the familiar case, boiling at 351.1 K against water's 373 K.

A negative deviation does the reverse and gives a MAXIMUM boiling azeotrope, and a solution with no deviation is ideal and forms no azeotrope at all.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: The relative lowering of vapour pressure of an aqueous solution containing non-volatile solute is \(0{\cdot}0225\). The mole fraction of the non-volatile solute is :
rows.solution:
The mole fraction of the solute is \(0{\cdot}0225\) — the same number as the relative lowering.

Raoult's law for a solution of a non-volatile solute states it directly:
\(\dfrac{p^{\,\circ} - p_s}{p^{\,\circ}} = x_2\)

that is, the RELATIVE lowering of vapour pressure EQUALS the mole fraction of the solute. No arithmetic is required; the quantity asked for is the quantity given.

Both sides are dimensionless, which is a check on the reasoning: a ratio of two pressures can only equal something that is itself a pure number, and a mole fraction is.

The other options are there for a student who sets up some calculation that the question does not call for — the value 0.80 or 0.725 would be the mole fraction of the SOLVENT if the number given had been something else entirely.

rows.stem: During electrolysis of aqueous solution of NaCl :
rows.solution:
HYDROGEN IS LIBERATED AT THE CATHODE.

The cathode is where reduction happens, and the two candidates are the sodium ion and water:
\(\mathrm{Na^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}\), \(E^{\circ} = -2{\cdot}71\) V
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\), \(E^{\circ} = -0{\cdot}83\) V

The species with the HIGHER reduction potential is reduced preferentially, and \(-0{\cdot}83\) is far higher, so water is reduced and hydrogen comes off. Sodium is not deposited at all — which disposes of one option.

At the ANODE chlorine is evolved, not oxygen. The potentials alone would predict oxygen (\(+1{\cdot}23\) against chlorine's \(+1{\cdot}36\)), but liberating oxygen carries a substantial OVERPOTENTIAL that more than wipes out its advantage. So the oxygen option is wrong, and the chlorine option is wrong only in naming the electrode — chlorine appears at the anode, never the cathode.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The addition of catalyst during a chemical reaction alters which of the following quantities of the reaction ?
rows.solution:
A catalyst alters the ACTIVATION ENERGY.

It works by providing an ALTERNATIVE PATH with a lower energy barrier, so a larger fraction of molecules carries enough energy to react and the rate rises. What it does not do is change where the reaction starts or finishes.

Enthalpy, entropy and internal energy are all state functions of the reactants and products. A catalyst changes neither, so \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta S\) and \(\Delta G\) are exactly what they were, and the EQUILIBRIUM CONSTANT is unchanged with them.

That is the essential point: a catalyst changes how FAST equilibrium is reached, never WHERE it lies. It also lowers the barrier in both directions equally, so forward and backward reactions are accelerated to the same degree.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: For the elementary reaction \(\mathrm{P} \rightarrow \mathrm{Q}\), the rate of disappearance of 'P' increases by a factor of 8 upon doubling the concentration of 'P'. The order of the reaction with respect to 'P' is :
rows.solution:
The order with respect to \(\mathrm{P}\) is 3.

Doubling the concentration multiplies the rate by \(2^n\), where \(n\) is the order:
\(8 = 2^n\)
and since \(8 = 2^3\), the order is 3.

A note on the wording. The question calls this an ELEMENTARY reaction \(\mathrm{P} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Q}\), and for a genuinely elementary step the order equals the molecularity — which for a single molecule of \(\mathrm{P}\) breaking up would be 1, not 3. The stated data and the word "elementary" therefore cannot both hold. The answer is read from the DATA, which is what order always rests on.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aliphatic primary amines can be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution with anion formed by phthalimide.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Gabriel phthalimide synthesis does give aliphatic primary amines, and the Reason names the step on which the whole method turns.

Potassium hydroxide removes phthalimide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, made acidic by the two carbonyl groups flanking it. The ANION so formed is a good nucleophile, and it attacks the alkyl halide in a nucleophilic substitution, giving N-alkylphthalimide; hydrolysis then frees the amine:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2}\)

The method's value is that it gives a PURE primary amine, with no secondary or tertiary contamination. It works only for ALIPHATIC amines, because an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution — which is why the Assertion is careful to say "aliphatic".

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Uracil base is present in DNA.
Reason (R) : DNA undergoes self-replication.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

URACIL is not present in DNA. Both nucleic acids carry adenine, guanine and cytosine, but the fourth base differs: DNA has THYMINE where RNA has uracil. So the Assertion fails on a simple point of fact.

The Reason is correct — DNA does undergo self-replication, each strand serving as the template for its complement, which is how genetic information passes from one generation to the next.

The two statements are also unrelated. Replication depends on the COMPLEMENTARY PAIRING of bases, not on which particular base occupies the fourth slot, so even a corrected Assertion would not follow from the Reason.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
Reason (R) : Diazonium salts of aliphatic amines show resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Aromatic diazonium salts ARE the more stable. Benzenediazonium chloride survives at 273-278 K and can even be isolated as a solid, whereas an aliphatic diazonium salt breaks up the moment it forms, with brisk effervescence of nitrogen.

But the Reason attaches the resonance to the wrong compound. It is the AROMATIC diazonium ion that is stabilised by resonance — its positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring. An ALIPHATIC diazonium ion has no ring to spread the charge over, so it shows no such stabilisation at all.

Corrected — resonance in the AROMATIC salt — the Reason would have explained the Assertion exactly. As written it names the opposite compound.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(p\)-nitroaniline is a weaker base than \(p\)-toluidine.
Reason (R) : The electron withdrawing effect of \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) group in \(p\)-nitroaniline makes it a weaker base.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

p-Nitroaniline is much the weaker base — \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) about 13 against p-toluidine's 8.9.

The Reason gives the cause exactly. The nitro group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, and from the PARA position it can draw the nitrogen's lone pair right onto its own oxygen by resonance, as well as pulling inductively. A lone pair partly committed elsewhere is less available to accept a proton, so the base is weakened.

The methyl group of p-toluidine does the opposite: it releases electron density towards the ring and so towards the nitrogen, making p-toluidine a slightly STRONGER base than aniline itself.

Note that this question's sibling in another set prints the nitro group as "electron donating", which makes its Reason false and its answer different. One word decides it.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A 6% solution of glucose (molar mass = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) is isotonic with \(2{\cdot}5\%\) solution of an unknown organic substance. Calculate the molecular weight of the unknown organic substance.
rows.solution:
ISOTONIC means the two solutions have the SAME osmotic pressure. Since \(\Pi = CRT\) and both are at the same temperature, equal osmotic pressure means equal MOLAR CONCENTRATION:
\(C_{\text{glucose}} = C_{\text{unknown}}\)

Both percentages are mass per unit volume, and both refer to the same volume, so the concentrations may be compared as moles per that volume — mass divided by molar mass:
\(\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{G}}}{M_{\mathrm{G}}} = \dfrac{w_{\mathrm{U}}}{M_{\mathrm{U}}}\)
\(\dfrac{6}{180} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5}{M_{\mathrm{U}}}\)

\(M_{\mathrm{U}} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5 \times 180}{6}\)

\(M_{\mathrm{U}} = 75\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The result makes sense as a check: the unknown is present at less than half the mass of the glucose yet gives the same number of moles, so its molar mass must be less than half of 180 — and 75 is.

rows.stem:
A first order reaction has a rate constant \(1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). How long will 5 g of this reactant take to reduce to \(2{\cdot}5\) g ?
[ log 2 = \(0{\cdot}301\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}4771\), log 4 = \(0{\cdot}6021\) ]
rows.solution:
The amount falls from 5 g to 2.5 g, which is exactly HALF — so the time asked for is the half-life. Use the first order equation:

\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranging for \(t\), with the ratio \(5/2{\cdot}5 = 2\):
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 2 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}301}{1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(t = \dfrac{0{\cdot}6932}{1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(t = 554{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{s}\), that is \(5{\cdot}54 \times 10^{2}\) s

Note that MASSES may be used in place of concentrations here, because only their RATIO enters and the volume cancels. And the shortcut is worth seeing: \(t_{1/2} = 0{\cdot}693/k\) gives the same answer in one line, which is why the logarithms of 3 and 4 supplied with the question are not needed.

rows.stem: What is lanthanoid contraction ? Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction. Why ?
rows.solution:
LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is the steady DECREASE in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series, from lanthanum to lutetium, as the atomic number increases.

The cause is poor shielding. Each added electron goes into a \(4f\) orbital, and \(4f\) orbitals are diffuse and shield the nuclear charge badly. So each added proton pulls the outer electrons in a little harder than the added electron pushes them out, and the radius shrinks step by step.

WHY THE ACTINOID CONTRACTION IS STEEPER. The same mechanism operates, but the \(5f\) orbitals shield EVEN MORE POORLY than the \(4f\) orbitals do — they are more diffuse still and reach further out from the nucleus. The net inward pull per element is therefore larger, and the contraction from one element to the next is greater.

The best-known consequence of the lanthanoid contraction is that zirconium and hafnium end up with almost identical radii, which makes them notoriously hard to separate.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Why do transition metals have high enthalpy of atomization ? Which element of 3d-series has lowest enthalpy of atomization ?
rows.solution:
Because in a transition metal the \((n-1)d\) ELECTRONS TAKE PART IN THE METALLIC BONDING alongside the \(ns\) electrons.

Enthalpy of atomisation measures the energy needed to pull the atoms of a metal apart into free gaseous atoms — in other words, to overcome the metallic bonding. With more electrons involved in that bonding, the interatomic interaction is stronger and the energy required is greater. The effect peaks in the middle of the series, where the number of unpaired d electrons is largest.

ZINC has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the 3d series.

Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its d subshell is completely filled, so those electrons are paired and take no part in the bonding. Only the two \(4s\) electrons do, the interatomic forces are correspondingly weak, and zinc atomises at only about 126 kJ per mole against chromium's 397.

rows.stem:
(a) In the following pair of compounds, which compound undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction faster and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - CH_2 - I}\) OR \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - CH_2 - Br}\)
(b) Write the major product in the following :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5 - CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cl_2},\ \text{UV light}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — BOTH sub-parts are printed as DRAWINGS. (a) prints the pair as two SKELETAL ZIGZAGS, each of exactly three line segments with the halogen letter set at the upper-right terminus ("I" on the left one, "Br" on the right), the word OR between them — i.e. a three-carbon chain bearing the halogen, transcribed above as the condensed n-propyl halide. (Segment count checked at 3x on the paper AND against the marking scheme's reprint of the same structure on ms/p03, which agrees at three segments.) (b) prints a skeletal benzene ring bonded to the label "CH2CH3", with a long reaction arrow labelled "Cl2 , UV light" and no product shown. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) 1-IODOPROPANE reacts faster.

With the same carbon skeleton in both, the only variable is how good a leaving group the halogen makes. In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the carbon-halogen bond breaks as the nucleophile attacks, so the WEAKER that bond, the faster the reaction.

The \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is weaker than the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond, because iodine is the larger atom and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well. The iodide ion is also the more stable of the two anions, being larger and better able to spread its charge — a better leaving group in both senses.

The order for the whole group runs iodide, bromide, chloride, fluoride.

(b) Chlorine with ULTRAVIOLET LIGHT and no catalyst attacks the SIDE CHAIN, not the ring — these are free radical conditions, and a chlorine radical abstracts the hydrogen it can take most easily.

That is the BENZYLIC hydrogen, on the carbon attached to the ring, because the radical left behind is delocalised into the ring. Of the ethyl group's two carbons, only the first is benzylic.

Major product: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH(Cl){-}CH_3}\), 1-chloro-1-phenylethane.

Had the conditions been chlorine with iron in the dark, the substitution would have been on the RING instead.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Denaturation of protein
(b) Invert sugar
rows.solution:
(a) DENATURATION OF PROTEIN is the loss of a protein's BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY when its native structure is destroyed by a physical change such as heating, or a chemical one such as a change in pH.

The weak forces holding the chain in shape — hydrogen bonds and other interactions — are disrupted, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds. The SECONDARY and TERTIARY structures are destroyed, while the PRIMARY structure survives intact, since no peptide bond is broken. Coagulation of egg white on boiling is the everyday instance.

(b) INVERT SUGAR is the equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose obtained by hydrolysing sucrose.

The name records a change in OPTICAL ROTATION. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, \(+66{\cdot}5^{\circ}\); hydrolysis gives glucose at \(+52{\cdot}5^{\circ}\) and fructose at \(-92{\cdot}4^{\circ}\), and the fructose dominates, so the mixture is LAEVOrotatory overall, about \(-20^{\circ}\). The sign of rotation is inverted, and the product is named for it.

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - Br} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\text{Partial hydrolysis}]{\mathrm{OH^{-}}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{Br_2}} \mathrm{C}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[273 - 278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2} + \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{C}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In (b) the starting material is PRINTED AS A DRAWING — a skeletal benzene ring with the label "NO2" above it — not as the condensed formula transcribed above. Sub-part (a) is printed as ordinary condensed formulae and needs no crop. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) Potassium cyanide substitutes for the bromide, giving the NITRILE. Note the carbon count rising from two to three:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\), propanenitrile

PARTIAL hydrolysis stops at the AMIDE. Complete hydrolysis would go on to the carboxylic acid, so the word "partial" is doing real work here:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2}\), propanamide

Bromine with alkali is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, which converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine

The sequence adds a carbon and then removes one — a roundabout route to an amine of the same chain length, but one that guarantees a pure primary product.

(b) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid generated in situ at 273-278 K diazotises it. The low temperature is essential — above about 278 K the salt decomposes to phenol:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

Ethanol reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by hydrogen and being itself oxidised to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_6}\), benzene

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the reaction involved in the following :
(a) Wolff-Kishner reduction
(b) Decarboxylation reaction
(c) Cannizzaro reaction
rows.solution:
(a) WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), in two stages. Hydrazine first condenses with it to give the hydrazone, and heating that with a strong base in a high boiling solvent expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N{-}NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)
It is the alkaline counterpart of Clemmensen reduction, which does the same job in acid.

(b) DECARBOXYLATION removes the carboxyl group as carbonate, leaving a hydrocarbon with ONE CARBON FEWER. The sodium salt of the acid is heated with soda lime — sodium hydroxide with calcium oxide:
\(\mathrm{R{-}COONa} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NaOH}\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{R{-}H} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)
It works equally for an aryl salt, sodium benzoate giving benzene.

(c) CANNIZZARO REACTION is the disproportionation of an aldehyde that has NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen: with concentrated alkali, one molecule is reduced to the alcohol while another is oxidised to the salt of the acid.
\(2\mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOO^-Na^+}\)
Benzaldehyde behaves the same way, giving benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate. The absence of an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is essential — an aldehyde that has one undergoes aldol instead.

rows.stem:
Give the equations of reactions for the preparation of : (any three)
(a) Phenol from chlorobenzene
(b) Salicylaldehyde from phenol
(c) 2-Methoxyacetophenone from anisole
(d) Picric acid from phenol
rows.solution:
(a) PHENOL FROM CHLOROBENZENE — the Dow process. The conditions are severe because an aryl halide resists nucleophilic substitution:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} \xrightarrow[623\ \mathrm{K},\ 300\ \mathrm{atm}]{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)

(b) SALICYLALDEHYDE FROM PHENOL — the Reimer-Tiemann reaction. Chloroform with alkali generates dichlorocarbene, which attacks the phenoxide ion at its ORTHO position; acidification then frees the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)

(c) 2-METHOXYACETOPHENONE FROM ANISOLE — a Friedel-Crafts acylation. The methoxy group is activating and ortho, para directing, and the ORTHO product is the one named:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3O{-}C_6H_4{-}COCH_3}\)

(d) PICRIC ACID FROM PHENOL. Concentrated nitric acid nitrates all three activated positions:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH}\)
The product, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, is a genuinely strong acid — three nitro groups pull electron density away and stabilise the anion enormously.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Chlorine is ortho/para directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions, though chlorine is an electron withdrawing group.
(b) Racemic mixture is optically inactive.
(c) Allyl chloride is hydrolysed more readily than n-propyl chloride.
rows.solution:
(a) Because chlorine acts on the ring by TWO OPPOSING EFFECTS, and they govern different things.

Its INDUCTIVE effect withdraws electron density from the whole ring, which makes every position less reactive than in benzene — so chlorine is DEACTIVATING, and that is the part the question notices.

Its RESONANCE effect does the opposite and is position-selective. The chlorine's lone pair is donated into the ring, and the structures that result place negative charge specifically at the ORTHO and PARA positions. Those positions therefore retain more electron density than the meta position, and they also give the more stable carbocation intermediate when an electrophile attacks there.

So the two effects divide the labour: the inductive effect decides HOW FAST (slower than benzene), the resonance effect decides WHERE (ortho and para). A substituent can be deactivating and ortho, para directing at once.

(b) Because a racemic mixture contains the two ENANTIOMERS IN EQUAL AMOUNTS.

Each enantiomer rotates plane polarised light by the same angle but in OPPOSITE directions. With equal numbers of each in the beam's path, one rotation exactly cancels the other and the net rotation is zero.

The compensation is EXTERNAL — between molecules, not within them. Each molecule is still optically active on its own; it is only the mixture that shows nothing.

(c) Because the carbocation formed from allyl chloride is stabilised by RESONANCE.

Hydrolysis here proceeds through a carbocation, and the slow step is forming it. Allyl chloride's halogen sits on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so when the chloride leaves the positive charge is delocalised over TWO carbons — two equivalent resonance structures share it.

n-Propyl chloride gives a plain primary carbocation with no such help. A more stable intermediate means a lower barrier and a faster reaction.

rows.stem: The vapour pressure of a solvent at 283 K is 100 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of a dilute solution containing 1 mole of a strong electrolyte AB in 50 moles of the solvent at 283 K (assuming complete dissociation of solute AB).
rows.solution:
The electrolyte dissociates completely into two ions, so the van't Hoff factor is \(i = 2\) and the particle count is DOUBLE what the formula suggests.

For a dilute solution, Raoult's law with the van't Hoff correction gives
\(\dfrac{p^{\,\circ} - p_s}{p^{\,\circ}} = i \times \dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}}\)

Substituting \(p^{\,\circ} = 100\) mm Hg, 1 mole of \(\mathrm{AB}\) and 50 moles of solvent:
\(\dfrac{100 - p_s}{100} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{50} = 0{\cdot}04\)
\(100 - p_s = 4\)

\(p_s = 96\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Forgetting the factor of 2 is the trap; it would give 98 mm Hg. The dissociation DOUBLES the lowering, because a colligative property counts PARTICLES and one formula unit of \(\mathrm{AB}\) supplies two of them.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell :
\(\mathrm{Zn\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\ (0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Sn^{2+}}\ (0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Sn\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\), \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Sn^{2+}/Sn}} = -0{\cdot}14\ \mathrm{V}\)
[ log 10 = 1 ]
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so zinc is oxidised and tin is deposited at the cathode — consistent with zinc's being the more negative of the two potentials.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = (-0{\cdot}14) - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}62\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Sn^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Sn}\), so \(n = 2\), and the solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}62 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{0{\cdot}001}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}62 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10^{2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}62 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 2 = 0{\cdot}62 - 0{\cdot}059\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}561\ \mathrm{V}\)

The correction is NEGATIVE because the product ion is at the higher concentration, which pushes the reaction slightly the wrong way — a small effect, since the Nernst term is only about a tenth of a volt even for a hundredfold ratio.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a gaseous reaction triples when temperature is increased from \(17\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Calculate the energy of activation for this reaction.
[Given : \(2{\cdot}303\ \mathrm{R} = 19{\cdot}15\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}48\)]
rows.solution:
Two rate constants at two temperatures are related by the Arrhenius equation in its two-point form:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

Convert the temperatures: \(17\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 290\) K and \(27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 300\) K. The rate TRIPLES, so \(k_2/k_1 = 3\) and \(\log 3 = 0{\cdot}48\):

\(0{\cdot}48 = \dfrac{E_a}{19{\cdot}15}\left[\dfrac{300 - 290}{290 \times 300}\right] = \dfrac{E_a}{19{\cdot}15} \times \dfrac{10}{87000}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0{\cdot}48 \times 19{\cdot}15 \times 290 \times 300}{10}\)

\(E_a = 79970\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(79{\cdot}97\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Two points of care. The temperatures MUST be in kelvin — using 17 and 27 would give a wildly different answer, since their ratio is nothing like 290/300. And note how small a temperature change this is: ten degrees near room temperature roughly triples the rate, which is the familiar rule of thumb this calculation puts a number to.

rows.stem: What are reducing sugars ?
rows.context: Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. On the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, i.e., they are oxidized by Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution. A monosaccharide like glucose is aldohexose and its molecular formula was found to be \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\). After reacting with different reagents like HI, \(\mathrm{H_2N - OH}\), Bromine water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\), etc. its structure was found to contain one aldehyde group, one primary alcoholic group, \((-\mathrm{CH_2OH})\) and four secondary alcoholic groups \((>\mathrm{CHOH})\). Despite having the aldehyde group, glucose does not give some of the reactions of aldehyde group like Schiff's test, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition. This explains the existence of glucose in two cyclic hemiacetal forms which differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C \(-\) 1.
rows.solution:
REDUCING SUGARS are those that REDUCE Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution — giving a silver mirror with the first and a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide with the second.

What makes a sugar reducing is a FREE ANOMERIC CARBON: one whose hydroxyl is not tied up in a glycosidic link. Such a ring can open in solution to the straight-chain form and expose a free aldehyde group, and it is that group which reduces the reagent.

All MONOsaccharides are reducing, aldoses and ketoses alike. Among the disaccharides, maltose and lactose are reducing because one anomeric carbon is left free, while SUCROSE is not — there the link runs between the anomeric carbons of BOTH units, so neither ring can open.

rows.stem:
Classify the following into monosaccharide and disaccharide :
Fructose, Sucrose, Lactose, Galactose
rows.context: Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. On the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, i.e., they are oxidized by Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution. A monosaccharide like glucose is aldohexose and its molecular formula was found to be \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\). After reacting with different reagents like HI, \(\mathrm{H_2N - OH}\), Bromine water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\), etc. its structure was found to contain one aldehyde group, one primary alcoholic group, \((-\mathrm{CH_2OH})\) and four secondary alcoholic groups \((>\mathrm{CHOH})\). Despite having the aldehyde group, glucose does not give some of the reactions of aldehyde group like Schiff's test, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition. This explains the existence of glucose in two cyclic hemiacetal forms which differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C \(-\) 1.
rows.solution:
MONOSACCHARIDES: FRUCTOSE and GALACTOSE. Each is a single sugar unit and cannot be hydrolysed to anything simpler.

DISACCHARIDES: SUCROSE and LACTOSE. Each is two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic linkage, and hydrolysis splits each into two.

Sucrose gives glucose and fructose; lactose gives glucose and galactose. Note that the two products of sucrose and one product of lactose appear in this very list, which is the pattern the question is testing — a disaccharide is built from the monosaccharides beside it.

rows.stem: Name the polysaccharide which is known as 'animal starch'. Why is it called 'animal starch' ?
rows.context: Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. On the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, i.e., they are oxidized by Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution. A monosaccharide like glucose is aldohexose and its molecular formula was found to be \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\). After reacting with different reagents like HI, \(\mathrm{H_2N - OH}\), Bromine water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\), etc. its structure was found to contain one aldehyde group, one primary alcoholic group, \((-\mathrm{CH_2OH})\) and four secondary alcoholic groups \((>\mathrm{CHOH})\). Despite having the aldehyde group, glucose does not give some of the reactions of aldehyde group like Schiff's test, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition. This explains the existence of glucose in two cyclic hemiacetal forms which differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C \(-\) 1.
rows.solution:
The polysaccharide known as ANIMAL STARCH is GLYCOGEN.

The name records what it does and what it is like. Carbohydrate is stored in the ANIMAL body as glycogen, in the liver and in muscle, exactly as plants store it as starch — and when the blood sugar falls, enzymes break glycogen back down to glucose.

STRUCTURALLY it closely resembles AMYLOPECTIN, the branched component of starch: a polymer of \(\alpha\)-glucose units joined by \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linkages along the chains with \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_6}\) linkages at the branch points. Glycogen is simply MORE highly branched still.

The heavy branching is functional: many chain ends mean many places for enzymes to start, so glucose can be released quickly when it is wanted.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the isomers of glucose which in the cyclic form differ only in the configuration of the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group at C \(-\) 1.
(ii) Presence of which functional group was detected when glucose reacted with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water ?
rows.context: Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. On the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, i.e., they are oxidized by Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution. A monosaccharide like glucose is aldohexose and its molecular formula was found to be \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\). After reacting with different reagents like HI, \(\mathrm{H_2N - OH}\), Bromine water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\), etc. its structure was found to contain one aldehyde group, one primary alcoholic group, \((-\mathrm{CH_2OH})\) and four secondary alcoholic groups \((>\mathrm{CHOH})\). Despite having the aldehyde group, glucose does not give some of the reactions of aldehyde group like Schiff's test, \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition. This explains the existence of glucose in two cyclic hemiacetal forms which differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C \(-\) 1.
rows.solution:
(i) They are the ANOMERS of glucose — \(\alpha\)-D-GLUCOSE and \(\beta\)-D-GLUCOSE.

When glucose closes into its ring, \(\mathrm{C_1}\) becomes a new stereocentre, carrying four different groups where it had a double bond before. The new hydroxyl can end up on either side of the ring: BELOW the plane in the \(\alpha\) form, ABOVE it in the \(\beta\) form. Everything else about the two molecules is identical, and \(\mathrm{C_1}\) is accordingly called the ANOMERIC carbon.

In solution the two interconvert through the open-chain form, which is what MUTAROTATION is — the gradual drift of the observed rotation towards an equilibrium value.

(ii) The ALDEHYDE group, \(-\mathrm{CHO}\).

Bromine water oxidises glucose to the six carbon gluconic acid. It is a MILD oxidising agent, too mild to attack a hydroxyl group, so the only thing in the molecule it can have oxidised is the aldehyde — and that specificity is what makes the reaction a proof.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: On what basis can we say that Cu is a transition element but Zn is not ? (Atomic number : Cu = 29, Zn = 30)
rows.context:
Transition metals have incomplete d-subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. The presence of partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from that of the non-transition elements. With partly filled d-orbitals, these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands. The transition metals and their compounds also exhibit catalytic properties and paramagnetic behaviour. The transition metals are very hard and have low volatility. An examination of the \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values shows the varying trends :

|  | \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) |
|---|---|
| V | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Cr | \(-0{\cdot}91\) |
| Mn | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Fe | \(-0{\cdot}44\) |
| Co | \(-0{\cdot}28\) |
| Ni | \(-0{\cdot}25\) |
| Cu | \(+0{\cdot}34\) |
| Zn | \(-0{\cdot}76\) |
rows.solution:
Because COPPER has an incompletely filled d subshell in one of its stable oxidation states and ZINC never does.

A transition element is defined as one with a partly filled d subshell in the neutral ATOM or in one of its STABLE IONS.

Copper is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^1\), so as the atom its subshell is full — but \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), its commonest ion, is \(3d^9\), which is PARTLY filled. The definition is satisfied, and copper shows all the characteristic behaviour: coloured compounds, variable oxidation state, catalytic activity.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^2\), and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — completely filled in both. Zinc has no stable state with a partly filled subshell, so it is NOT a transition element; its compounds are white, diamagnetic, and confined to the \(+2\) state.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Why do transition elements show variety of oxidation states ?
rows.context:
Transition metals have incomplete d-subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. The presence of partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from that of the non-transition elements. With partly filled d-orbitals, these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands. The transition metals and their compounds also exhibit catalytic properties and paramagnetic behaviour. The transition metals are very hard and have low volatility. An examination of the \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values shows the varying trends :

|  | \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) |
|---|---|
| V | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Cr | \(-0{\cdot}91\) |
| Mn | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Fe | \(-0{\cdot}44\) |
| Co | \(-0{\cdot}28\) |
| Ni | \(-0{\cdot}25\) |
| Cu | \(+0{\cdot}34\) |
| Zn | \(-0{\cdot}76\) |
rows.solution:
Because the \((n-1)d\) AND \(ns\) SUBSHELLS LIE AT COMPARABLE ENERGIES, so electrons from BOTH can be used in bonding.

In a main-group element only the outermost \(s\) and \(p\) electrons are accessible; the shell below is far too tightly held. In a transition element the \((n-1)d\) orbitals sit close in energy to the \(ns\), and there is no sharp threshold at which the supply of available electrons stops.

So an element may lose only its \(ns\) electrons, or some of its \(d\) electrons as well, and many intermediate states are possible. Manganese runs from \(+2\) to \(+7\) for exactly this reason.

The closeness in energy also means the states differ by ONE at a time, whereas a main-group element's states typically differ by two.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Why do \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values show irregular trend from Vanadium to Zinc ?
(ii) How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of the non-transition elements ?
rows.context:
Transition metals have incomplete d-subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. The presence of partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from that of the non-transition elements. With partly filled d-orbitals, these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands. The transition metals and their compounds also exhibit catalytic properties and paramagnetic behaviour. The transition metals are very hard and have low volatility. An examination of the \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values shows the varying trends :

|  | \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) |
|---|---|
| V | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Cr | \(-0{\cdot}91\) |
| Mn | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Fe | \(-0{\cdot}44\) |
| Co | \(-0{\cdot}28\) |
| Ni | \(-0{\cdot}25\) |
| Cu | \(+0{\cdot}34\) |
| Zn | \(-0{\cdot}76\) |
rows.solution:
(i) Because \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}}\) is the net result of THREE energy terms, and two of them vary irregularly across the series.

Taking a metal to its aqueous \(+2\) ion requires sublimation — the enthalpy of atomisation — and then TWO ionisations; the energy released in hydrating the ion pays part of that back. The potential reflects the balance.

The sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies does not vary smoothly, because half-filled and filled d configurations are specially stable and distort the trend; the enthalpies of sublimation are irregular for the same reason. Hydration enthalpy varies fairly steadily with ionic size, but it cannot smooth out the other two.

Copper is the extreme case: its high enthalpy of atomisation and low hydration enthalpy leave it with the only POSITIVE value in the series.

(ii) In a TRANSITION metal the oxidation states differ by ONE — manganese shows \(+2\), \(+3\), \(+4\), \(+5\), \(+6\) and \(+7\), a continuous run.

In a NON-transition metal they differ by TWO — tin and lead show \(+2\) and \(+4\), thallium \(+1\) and \(+3\), with nothing in between.

The reason lies in which electrons are being removed. A main-group element loses its \(p\) electrons in a PAIR or keeps them; the s pair is removed together or not at all. A transition element draws on d electrons that are close in energy and individually accessible, so it can stop anywhere.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Of the \(\mathrm{d^4}\) species, \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly reducing while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly oxidizing. Why ? (Atomic number : Cr = 24, Mn = 25)
(ii) Complete the following ionic equation :
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^{-}} \longrightarrow\)
rows.context:
Transition metals have incomplete d-subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. The presence of partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from that of the non-transition elements. With partly filled d-orbitals, these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands. The transition metals and their compounds also exhibit catalytic properties and paramagnetic behaviour. The transition metals are very hard and have low volatility. An examination of the \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values shows the varying trends :

|  | \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) |
|---|---|
| V | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Cr | \(-0{\cdot}91\) |
| Mn | \(-1{\cdot}18\) |
| Fe | \(-0{\cdot}44\) |
| Co | \(-0{\cdot}28\) |
| Ni | \(-0{\cdot}25\) |
| Cu | \(+0{\cdot}34\) |
| Zn | \(-0{\cdot}76\) |
rows.solution:
(i) Both are \(d^4\) species, and in each case the driving force is the STABILITY OF THE NEIGHBOURING ION.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly REDUCING because losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral field the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Chromium(II) therefore gives that electron up readily, and giving electrons away is what a reducing agent does.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly OXIDISING because GAINING one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell, and unusually stable. Manganese(III) therefore takes an electron readily.

The two ions have the same d count and behave in opposite ways, because what each is reaching for lies on a different side of it.

(ii) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution permanganate is reduced only as far as manganese dioxide, while iodide is oxidised to iodate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} + \mathrm{IO_3^-}\)

Six electrons change hands: manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+4\), three each, while iodine climbs from \(-1\) to \(+5\). In ACID the permanganate would have gone all the way to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) instead — the medium decides the product.

rows.stem:
Answer any five of the following :
(a) How is the crystal field splitting energy for octahedral complex \((\Delta_{\mathrm{o}})\) related to that of tetrahedral complex \((\Delta_{\mathrm{t}})\) ?
(b) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2](NO_3)_2}\)
(c) Write the geometry and magnetic behaviour of the complex \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) on the basis of Valency Bond Theory (VBT).
(d) What type of isomerism is shown by the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]\,[Cr(CN)_6]}\) ?
(e) For the coordination compound on the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\). Is the coordination compound a high spin or low spin complex ?
(f) Out of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\), which complex is heteroleptic and why ?
(g) Draw the structures of optical isomers of \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}}\).
rows.solution:
(a) The two are related by
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} = \dfrac{4}{9}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\)

A tetrahedral field splits the d orbitals far less, for two reasons: there are only FOUR ligands instead of six, and none of them points directly at a d orbital. That small value is why tetrahedral complexes are almost always HIGH SPIN — \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}}\) is essentially never large enough to exceed the pairing energy.

(b) Two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) and two nitrate ions outside give \(-2\), so with two neutral diamine ligands platinum is \(+4\):
DICHLORIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)PLATINUM(IV) NITRATE

(c) In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\) with every electron paired and no inner orbital free; bonding uses the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\).
Hybridisation \(sp^3\), geometry TETRAHEDRAL, and with no unpaired electron the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

(d) COORDINATION ISOMERISM. Both the cation and the anion are complex ions, so the ligands can be swapped between the two metal centres — \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]}\) contain the same atoms differently distributed.

(e) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs LESS than pairing, so electrons spread out singly before any pair up. For \(d^4\):
\(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\)
with four unpaired electrons — a HIGH SPIN complex. Had \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) exceeded \(\mathrm{P}\), the configuration would have been \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^0\), low spin, with two.

(f) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\) is the heteroleptic one, because its metal is bound to MORE THAN ONE KIND of ligand — four ammonia molecules and two chlorides.
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) has only one kind of ligand throughout and is therefore HOMOLEPTIC.

(g) Only the CIS isomer of \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}}\) is optically active, and it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Each is an octahedron with the two chlorido ligands ADJACENT and the two diamine ligands spanning the remaining positions. The two structures are non-superimposable mirror images — dextro and laevo — related as a right hand is to a left. The TRANS isomer, with the chlorides opposite each other, has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(1) Oxidation of aldehydes is easier as compared to ketones.
(2) The alpha \((\alpha)\) hydrogen atoms of aldehydes are acidic in nature.
(ii) Write the products in the following reactions :
(1) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{I_2}} ? + ?\)
(2) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{(CH_3)_2Cd} \longrightarrow ? + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)
(iii) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between ethanoic acid and ethanal.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (ii) prints both substrates as DRAWINGS, not as the condensed formulae transcribed above: (1) a skeletal benzene ring with the label "COCH3" above it, arrow labelled "NaOH / I2" to "? + ?"; (2) a skeletal benzene ring with the label "COCl" above it, "+ (CH3)2Cd" then an arrow to "? + CdCl2". Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because oxidising an aldehyde requires only a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) BOND to be broken, while oxidising a ketone requires a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond to be broken.

An aldehyde has a hydrogen ON its carbonyl carbon. Oxidation removes that hydrogen and puts an oxygen in its place, and the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond is comparatively weak — which is why even a mild reagent such as Tollens' or Fehling's suffices.

A ketone has two carbon substituents there and no hydrogen at all. Oxidising it means CLEAVING the carbon chain, which needs a strong oxidising agent under drastic conditions and gives a mixture of shorter acids.

That difference is what makes Tollens' and Fehling's tests able to tell the two apart.

(2) Because the CARBANION left behind after the \(\alpha\)-hydrogen leaves is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

The carbonyl group is strongly electron withdrawing, so it pulls density away from the neighbouring carbon and weakens the bond to its hydrogen. More importantly, once that proton has gone the negative charge does not stay on the carbon: it is delocalised onto the carbonyl OXYGEN, an electronegative atom far better able to carry it.

A stabilised conjugate base means a stronger acid, so an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is acidic where an ordinary alkane hydrogen is not — and that acidity is what makes the aldol reaction and haloform reaction possible.

(ii)(1) Sodium hydroxide with iodine is the IODOFORM reaction, and acetophenone has the methyl group beside its carbonyl that the reaction requires. The methyl carbon leaves as iodoform and the rest becomes the salt of the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{I_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} + \mathrm{CHI_3}\)
The products are sodium benzoate and the yellow precipitate of iodoform.

(2) A dialkylcadmium is a MILD alkylating agent — mild enough to stop at the ketone instead of attacking it further, which is why it is preferred to a Grignard reagent here:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)
The product is acetophenone.

(iii) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warm each with sodium hydroxide and iodine: ETHANAL has a methyl group next to its carbonyl and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; ETHANOIC ACID has no carbonyl of that kind and gives none.

Tollens' reagent serves equally well the other way round — ethanal is an aldehyde and gives a silver mirror, while the acid does not. So does sodium hydrogencarbonate, which effervesces with the acid alone.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Draw structure of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone of benzaldehyde.
(ii) Arrange the following in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN :
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - COCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)
(iii) How can you convert phenyl magnesium bromide to benzoic acid ?
(iv) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between benzaldehyde and ethanal.
(v) Write the main product in the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - CO - CH_2 - COOC_2H_5} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaBH_4}} ?\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-part (v) the substrate is printed as a TWO-DIMENSIONAL structure — the chain "CH3 - C - CH2 - COOC2H5" with a vertical double bond dropping from the second carbon to an O written beneath it — which the linear transcription above renders as the condensed "CH3 - CO - CH2 - COOC2H5". Faithful in identity, but not what the page looks like. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(i) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water, so the product is benzaldehyde's carbon joined by a double bond to the nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)
The structure is a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{CH{=}N{-}NH}-\), joined to a second ring bearing nitro groups at positions 2 and 4. It is an orange crystalline solid, and its sharp melting point identifies the carbonyl compound it came from.

(ii) Reactivity towards a nucleophile falls as the carbonyl carbon is made less positive and more crowded, and alkyl groups do both. Increasing order:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

Ethanal has just one methyl group on its carbonyl carbon; propanone has two; and the tert-butyl ketone has a methyl and a bulky tert-butyl group, which both releases the most electron density and blocks the approach most completely.

(iii) Treat the Grignard reagent with CARBON DIOXIDE in dry ether, then hydrolyse:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} + \mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)
Solid carbon dioxide is usually used. The carbanion-like carbon of the reagent attacks the electron-poor carbon of the dioxide, adding ONE carbon and putting the carboxyl group on the ring.

(iv) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warm each with sodium hydroxide and iodine: ETHANAL has a methyl group next to its carbonyl and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; BENZALDEHYDE has a phenyl group there and gives none.

The Fehling's test distinguishes them too, and the other way round: ethanal, an aliphatic aldehyde, gives the red precipitate, while benzaldehyde, being aromatic, does not.

(v) Sodium borohydride is a MILD reducing agent: it reduces aldehydes and ketones but NOT esters, whose carbonyl is deactivated by resonance donation from the ester oxygen.

The substrate carries both, so only the KETONE is attacked:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(OH){-}CH_2{-}COOC_2H_5}\)
The ketone \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) has become \(\mathrm{CH{-}OH}\) and the ester group is untouched. Lithium aluminium hydride would have reduced both.

rows.stem:
(i) The resistance of \(0{\cdot}05\) M \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) solution is found to be 100 ohm. If the cell constant is \(0{\cdot}0354\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), calculate the molar conductivity of the acetic acid solution.
(ii) State Faraday's first law of electrolysis. How much charge in Faraday is required for the reduction of 1 mol of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) The cell constant converts a measured resistance into a conductivity:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}0354\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{100\ \Omega}\)
\(\kappa = 3{\cdot}54 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

Molar conductivity then refers that to one mole of electrolyte, so the concentration divides out:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}54 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}05}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 7{\cdot}08\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The figure is worth a second look. A strong electrolyte at this concentration would give something in the hundreds; 7.08 against acetic acid's limiting value of 390 says the acid is barely 2% dissociated — which is exactly what makes it a weak acid.

(ii) FARADAY'S FIRST LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS. The amount of chemical reaction occurring at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte. In symbols \(m = ZIt\), where \(Z\) is the electrochemical equivalent, \(I\) the current and \(t\) the time.

For the reduction asked about, count the change in oxidation state. In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) the four oxides give \(-8\) against an overall \(-1\), so manganese is \(+7\); in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) it is \(+2\). Each manganese gains FIVE electrons:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

One mole of permanganate needs 5 mol of electrons, that is 5 FARADAY.

rows.stem:
(i) The conductivity of \(0{\cdot}0025\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\) acetic acid is \(5{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation if \(\Lambda^{\mathrm{o}}_{\mathrm{m}}\) for acetic acid is \(390\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\).
(ii) Write anode, cathode and overall reaction of lead storage battery.
rows.solution:
(i) First convert conductivity to molar conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}0025}\)
\(\Lambda_m = 21\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of that to the limiting value, which is what the electrolyte would show if it were fully dissociated:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{21}{390}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}053\), that is about 5.3%

The smallness of the figure is the point: acetic acid is a WEAK electrolyte, and at this concentration only about one molecule in twenty is ionised at any moment. For a strong electrolyte the ratio would be close to 1, which is why this method of finding \(\alpha\) is used for weak electrolytes alone.

(ii) AT THE ANODE, lead is oxidised and the lead(II) formed is at once precipitated as the insoluble sulphate:
\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^-\)

AT THE CATHODE, lead dioxide is reduced, also ending as lead sulphate:
\(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

OVERALL:
\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

Both electrodes become coated with lead sulphate as the cell discharges, and the acid is consumed — which is why a discharged battery can be recognised from the fall in the density of its electrolyte. Recharging drives all of this backwards.
